def solution(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    # From the examples:
    # True cases:
    # (1000, -2) -> -2
    # (-99, 0) -> -99
    # (-1000, 0) -> -1000
    # (10, 99) -> 10
    # (-99, 1) -> -99
    #
    # False cases:
    # (10, -1000) -> -999 (False)
    # (99, 2) -> 3 (False)
    # (-1, 1) -> 0 (False)
    # (2, -10) -> -9 (False)
    # (1000, 2) -> 3 (False)
    #
    # Observing the True cases, the output equals either a or b.
    # In True cases, output equals the minimum of a and b.
    # Check if output == min(a,b) in True cases:
    # (1000, -2) -> -2 == min(1000,-2) True
    # (-99, 0) -> -99 == min(-99,0) True
    # (-1000, 0) -> -1000 == min(-1000,0) True
    # (10, 99) -> 10 == min(10,99) True
    # (-99, 1) -> -99 == min(-99,1) True
    #
    # Check False cases:
    # (10, -1000) -> -999 != min(10,-1000) which is -1000, so False
    # (99, 2) -> 3 != min(99,2) which is 2, False
    # (-1, 1) -> 0 != min(-1,1) which is -1, False
    # (2, -10) -> -9 != min(2,-10) which is -10, False
    # (1000, 2) -> 3 != min(1000,2) which is 2, False
    #
    # So the function returns the minimum of a and b.
    return min(a, b)
```
